Abstract
Owing to the tooth‐centered nature of most oral diseases, the tooth‐centric
radial plane of cone‐beam computed tomography (CBCT) depicts the
anatomical and pathological features along the long axis of the tooth, serving
as a crucial imaging modality in the diagnosis, treatment planning, and
prognosis of multiple oral diseases. However, reconstructing these standard
planes from CBCT is labor‐intensive, time‐consuming, and error‐prone due to
anatomical variances and multi‐center discrepancies. This study proposes an
expertise‐inspired artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline for the reconstruction of
the tooth‐centric radial plane. By emulating expert's workflow, this AI pipeline
acquires the optimized maxillary and mandibular cross sections, segments the
teeth for dental arch curve depiction, and reconstructs dental arch‐defined
tooth‐centric radial planes. A total of 420 CBCT scans from two independent
centers, comprising both healthy and diseased subjects, were collected for
model development and validation. Teeth on the optimized cross sections were
explicitly segmented even in the presence of various complex diseases,
resulting in precise dental arch curve depictions. The AI‐reconstructed tooth‐

INTRODUCTION
Oral diseases affect nearly 3.5 billion people, leading to
declines in life quality, discomfort, and even death,
resulting in significant health and economic burden.[1]
The WHO global strategy and action plan emphasizes the
early detection and prevention of multiple oral diseases to
promote oral health, including the use of dental imag-
ing.[2] The periapical X‐ray and panoramic radiography
display anteroposterior plain projections of dental struc-
tures, causing inevitable overlapping along the radial
direction of the dental arch. Cone‐beam computed to-
mography (CBCT) reconstructs the dentomaxillofacial
region three‐dimensionally; however, it requires pre-
scriptions of radial planes to visualize teeth and bone.[3]
Since major oral diseases are characterized by the tooth‐
centric progression, the CBCT planes along the radial
directions of dental arches, which avoid structure over-
lapping, are crucial for presenting key informative in-
sights into the diagnosis, screening, treatment planning,
and follow‐up of oral diseases.[4] For instance, peri-
odontitis, a prevalent chronic dental disease, typically
develops along the tooth's long axis.[5] Likewise, the
evaluation of available bone volume for dental implants is
significantly related to the alveolar bone adjacent to the
teeth (Figure 1a,b).[6] Therefore, deriving tooth‐centric
radial planes from CBCT is vital for oral healthcare
management, offering significant health and socioeco-
nomic value.
Despite the irreplaceable benefits that tooth‐centric
radial planes bring, manual reconstruction of these
planes is laborious, time‐consuming, and error‐prone.

maxillary

The final step involves reslicing the CBCT volume along
the radial direction of the dental arch curve at the tooth
centers.[7] Nonetheless, the unstandardized selections of
these cross sections induce the subjective errors. Chal-
lenges also exist in precise dental arch curve depiction
due to variances in tooth shapes, dentition misarrange-
ments and the presence of lesions. Different tooth types
introduce morphological heterogeneity, with small inter‐
class variance (e.g., the tooth #14 and #15 exhibit similar
shapes), whereas large intra‐class variances (e.g., large
difference between individuals with same teeth). The
morphological difference becomes more pronounced in
patients with multitudinous oral diseases or dental
treatment histories that exhibit diverse patterns with
complicated pathological features.[8] These minor errors
during the reconstruction steps may accumulate into
significant differences in the final tooth‐centric radial
planes, subsequently hindering their clinical utility.
Substantial biases exist among different clinical centers
and radiological devices, and inaccurate and unstan-
dardized plane reconstruction becomes an obstacle to the
interinstitutional communications and collaborations.[9]
These challenges restrict the widespread and standard-
ized use of the tooth‐centric radial planes (Figure 1c,d).
With the rapid progress of artificial intelligence (AI),
it has been widely applied in healthcare for its real‐time
response, precise performance and standardized opera-
tion.[10] Regarding AI‐empowered standard 2D plane
reconstruction from 3D medical images, the prevailing
approaches include reinforcement learning and regres-
sion. Yang and colleagues constructed a multi‐agent
reinforcement learning model to analyze the spatial re-
lationships among the proposed standard planes from
pelvic 3D ultrasound volumes.[11] Meanwhile, Blansti
applied the U‐Net based heatmap regression to localize

Although the existing AI techniques achieve satisfying
performance in ultrasonic and MR, these straightforward
algorithms may not realize the precise reconstruction of
tooth‐centric radial planes. On one hand, the reinforce-
ment learning framework may be ineffective for large
datasets
with
complicated
oral‐maxillofacial
struc-
tures.[14] On the other hand, the end‐to‐end regression of
the spatial relationship neglects task complexity and may
result in insufficient robustness. This highlights the need
to integrate expertise in clinical knowledge to improve
interpretability, robustness, and generalization capability.
To address the challenges in intelligent reconstruction
of tooth‐centric radial planes, this study develops an AI
pipeline in accordance with the clinical workflow, con-
sisting of a pre‐processing, a tooth instance segmentation
and a radial plane reconstruction module. By detecting
the corner points on the maximum intensity projection
(MIP) of CBCT, the proposed set of maxillary and
mandibular cross sections were acquired at approxi-
mately the cementoenamel junction (CEJ) levels. The
teeth on the cross sections were automatically segmented
via the preliminary prediction by Mask RCNN and the
subsequent alignment of misclassified masks through
prompts from adjacent sections. Optimized cross sections
were then selected according to preset rules based on
tooth segmentation. Consequently, precise individualized
dental arch curves were depicted to facilitate plane re-
constructions along the radial directions of the curves at
every tooth site. The performance of tooth segmentation,
dental arch curve depiction, and radial plane recon-
struction was evaluated on a multicenter dataset. To
assess the clinical utility of the proposed AI pipeline, the
rating of image quality, confusion experiments and dental
biometric measurements were conducted on these AI‐
reconstructed planes (Figure 2). The hypothesis of this
study is that the AI‐reconstructed tooth‐centric radial
planes are clinically applicable for oral healthcare man-
agement with high robustness and generalization ability.

RESULT
2.1

Characteristics of multi‐center
dataset
The internal cohort included 400 patients (177 male, 223
female, average age: 35.91  12.72 years), with 320 for
training and 80 for validation. The external cohort
included 20 patients (5 male, 15 female, average age:
43.15  15.82 years) for testing. A total of 58.75% and 50%
of patients from the two cohorts were partially edentu-
lous, with the mandibular molars being the most
frequently missing teeth. Impacted teeth (28.25%, 50%),
dental caries (27%, 30%) and periapical periodontitis
(25%, 35%) were the most prevalent oral diseases in the
internal and external cohorts, respectively. The most
common dental treatments included filling restorations
(33.25%, 45%), root canal therapy (30%, 50%) and dental
prosthesis (22.5%, 45%) the internal and external cohorts,
respectively (Table 1).
2.2
|
Precise tooth segmentation for
individual dental arch curve depiction
The proposed sets of maxillary and mandibular cross
sections were acquired at the CEJ level through the pre‐
processing module (Supporting Information S1: Figure
S1). On the internal validation set, the Mask RCNN
outperformed Mask DINO and Mask2Former across all
evaluation metrics (Figure 3a). Tooth segmentation by
Mask RCNN with tooth alignment yielded mean pixel
accuracy (PA) of 93.10% and 86.76%, Dice coefficients of
87.43% and 81.10% and mean intersection over union
(mIoU) of 82.61% and 76.37% on the internal validation
and external test sets, respectively (Figure 3b). The vi-
sualizations of tooth masks revealed favorable segmen-
tation in healthy and diseased conditions, including tooth
loss, impacted teeth and metal artifacts (Figure 3c).
Bland–Altman (B–A) plots showed that the chosen opti-
mized planes for dental arch curve depiction demon-
strated high consistency
with manual prescriptions
(Figure 4a). The automatically depicted maxillary and
mandibular dental arch curves exhibited forms generally
similar to those labeled by experts. However, metal arti-
facts and tooth abnormalities (e.g., impacted wisdom
teeth) slightly interfered with the depiction of the partial
region (Figure 4b). The mean point‐to‐point alignment
errors between the automated and manually depicted
dental arches were 1.93  1.19 mm and 2.32  1.41 mm
on
the
internal
validation
and
external
test
sets
(Figure 4c).

DISCUSSION
This study innovatively constructed an AI pipeline for fully
automatic tooth‐centric radial plane reconstruction, and
validated its robustness across healthy and disease condi-
tions of all tooth sites, demonstrating its generalization
ability on multicenter datasets. Guided by clinical work-
flows, each step in the AI pipeline gains interpretability.
The AI‐reconstructed tooth‐centric radial planes accu-
rately represented the physiological and pathological fea-
tures. Furthermore, the proposed AI pipeline achieved
expert‐level
performance
in
specific
plane
re-
constructions. The automatic, generalized and robust AI
pipeline for tooth‐centric radial plane reconstruction es-
tablishes
a
foundation
for
AI‐based
oral
health
management.

Previous studies have employed reinforcement learning
with multiple agents to search for optimal plane loca-
tions;
while
this
approach
offers
self‐adaptability,
exploring the entire 3D volume results in slow conver-
gence and lower stability.[11] Similarly, the U‐Net‐based
heatmap method adopted convolutional representations
of high‐level features, showing strong feature extraction
capabilities. However, this method suffers from high data
requirements and limited interpretability.[12] In this
study, the expertise‐guided multi‐step collaboration imi-
tates
the
expert's
operations,
avoiding
“black‐box”
induced
by
sophisticated
model
architecture.
For
instance, the reference point localizations are determined
using
robust
traditional
computer
vision
methods,
including MIP and Harris corner detection. Guided by
the dental arch curve knowledge, the supervised instance
segmentation, rather than semantic segmentation, is
adopted to control the errors in cases such as missing or
impacted teeth. Additionally, incorporating multicenter
data with healthy and diseased subjects effectively in-
creases data heterogeneity. Previous studies incline to
impose strict inclusion criteria, leading to high intra‐
dataset similarity and insufficient performance in com-
plex circumstances.[16] In this study, the high internal
heterogeneity from various centers, radiology settings,
disease distributions and medical histories allows the AI
pipeline to learn the task‐related features rather than
irrelevant variances.

Precise tooth instance
segmentation
Precise tooth segmentation provides accurate anatom-
ical
information
for
the
downstream
tooth
center
localization and individualized dental arch depiction.
This study developed a Mask RCNN‐based model for
tooth instance segmentation on cross sections with
abundant
heterogeneities,
validating
high
accuracy.
Compared to tooth segmentations on panoramic and
periapical radiographs, the instance segmentation on
the cross sections of CBCT is notably specific in that
the
posterior
teeth
with
multiple
roots
appear
as
different instances on a single section. Addressing this
challenge, root alignment is proven to correct the Mask
RCNN misjudgment. Additionally, the proposed sets of
cross sections enable the AI pipeline to select the
optimized section that fulfills clinical requirements.
Regarding individual depictions of dental arch curves,
previous studies indicate that missing teeth and metal
artifacts significantly increase errors in automatic dental
arch
curve
depiction.[17,
18]
The
point‐to‐point
alignment errors of dental arches were lower than
those in a previous study with complete dentitions.[8]
Despite this, the AI pipeline demonstrates favorable
performance in patients with missing teeth, metal arti-
facts and other tooth structural abnormalities.
3.3
|
Accurate planes reconstruction
Previous studies have succeeded in tooth‐bone recon-
struction using deep learning‐based 3D segmentation of
teeth and alveolar bone and 3D reconstruction of teeth
based on the crown/root fusion and registration of
CBCT and intraoral scan data.[19] Compared to these
existing techniques, the proposed AI pipeline presents
an efficient approach in dimensional reduction with low
computational load and reduced model parameters,
making it well‐suited for clinical deployment. Qualita-
tive and quantitative results indicate that the quality of
radial plane reconstruction is directly proportional to
tooth segmentation performance. Slightly inferior tooth
segmentation of the posterior and mandibular tooth re-
sults in lower plane reconstruction performance. This
study introduces angular and distance errors[20] that
jointly represent the spatial localization errors between
AI‐reconstructed and GT planes. Generally, the angular
and distance errors are smaller in the maxilla than in
the mandible, consistent with the cross‐sectional seg-
mentation performance. Notably, the angular and dis-
tance errors at the premolar sites, located at the arch
corner, tend to be smaller than those at the anterior and
posterior teeth. This may be attributed to the perpen-
dicular long axis of premolars to the occlusal plane,
while incisors and molars display inclination angles due
to shapes, missing teeth, and other factors.[7] Qualita-
tively, AI‐reconstructed
planes resemble GT planes
regardless of tooth positions and oral diseases. Even in
images with missing teeth or artifacts, the AI pipeline
can
accurately
reconstruct
the
tooth‐centric
radial
planes, demonstrating strong generalization abilities.
Therefore, when faced with new dental restoration
materials
such
as
zirconia‐based
composites,
hydroxyapatite‐based composites, and titanium implants
which may induce similar artifacts because of their
comparable material composition to traditional restora-
tion materials, the proposed AI pipeline is likely to
robustly
reconstruct
the
planes
as
well.[21–23]
The
ambiguous lesion boundaries and inaccurate quantita-
tive analysis brought about by mistaken radial plane
reconstruction can inevitably cause misdiagnosis of oral
diseases, while AI‐reconstructed planes of high quality
can contribute to precise diagnosis in complex situations
across centers and diseases.

3.4
|
Clinical utilities of AI‐
reconstructed planes
This study validated the utility of applying this AI pipe-
line in clinical settings. Dental experts with years of
clinical experience rated the AI‐reconstructed planes as
medium to high quality, indicating that they meet clinical
requirements. The merely lower scores by a junior
specialist may be because of the attention to minor tur-
bulence
in
non‐interested
areas.
Subjectively,
AI‐
reconstructed planes possess high similarity to GT ones,
potentially misleading experts in discriminating the im-
age types, with the identification accuracies in both ex-
periments
of
approximately
50%.
Overall,
the
AI‐
reconstructed tooth‐centric radial planes are convincing
for clinical practice adoption.
A significant clinical application of tooth‐centric
radial planes is measuring dental biometrics.[24, 25] AI‐
reconstructed planes were validated for precise quantifi-
cation on multiple regions (i.e., anterior and posterior
teeth, maxilla and mandible) and locations (coronal, root,
alveolar bone, etc.),[7] displaying minimal errors induced
by the reconstruction process.
A potential limitation of this study is that the pro-
posed AI pipeline was validated for performance and
clinical utility in only two independent centers. The
relatively small sample size may introduce bias in model
estimations. However, the inclusion of two geographi-
cally distinct centers may partially mitigate sampling
bias. Future studies are warranted to incorporate larger
numbers of centers to achieve the comprehensive vali-
dation of the AI pipeline.
3.5
|
Implications for intelligent oral
health management
The AI pipeline shows potential in broad applications
in dental and maxillofacial imaging, including fast
screening of root resorption in orthodontics and precise
follow‐up checks of alveolar crest level in periodontics,
etc. The performance of automatic biometric measure-
ments
corroborated
that
AI‐reconstructed
planes
contain consistent feature information. The combina-
tion of the radial plane reconstruction AI pipeline and
the downstream AI models indicates its potential for a
full‐stack
AI‐based
oral
health
management
tool.
Additionally, the clinically applicable AI pipeline for
tooth‐centric radial plane reconstruction is expected to
facilitate data sharing among centers, provide high‐
quality data for scientific research and teaching, and
ultimately
develop
full‐chain
AI‐based
oral
health
management.
4
|
CONCLUSIONS
The AI‐based pipeline is capable of accurately recon-
structing the tooth‐centric radial planes of all teeth in a
highly robust and generalizable manner. These AI‐
reconstructed planes are validated to be clinically appli-
cable in multicenter scenarios. It is promising to facilitate
the AI pipeline to improve oral health care in the intel-
ligent dentistry era.

|
MATERIALS AND METHODS
5.1
|
Study design and gold standard
acquisition
This multi‐center study received approval from the
Medical Ethics Committee of the Hospital of Stomatol-
ogy, Sun Yat‐sen University (N0. KQEC‐2020‐29‐06). Due
to its retrospective nature, the informed consent was
waived. CBCTs were collected from 10th July, 2019 to 20th
March, 2024 from Hospital of Stomatology, Sun Yat‐sen
University using VGi EVO (NewTom, Italy) as the in-
ternal cohort, and from Liangqinghua Dental Hospital
using Smart 3D‐X (LargeV, China) as the external cohort.
Exclusion criteria included patients under 18 years of age,
severe artifacts, or extensively edentulous conditions (loss
of more than six teeth per jaw). The gold standard tooth‐
centric radial planes of all teeth were acquired manually
using Mimics (Materialise, Belgium) by a senior dental
specialist.
5.2
|
Development of expertise‐inspired
AI pipeline
The AI pipeline for tooth‐centric radial plane recon-
struction is designed by mimicking expertise workflow (i.
e., select optimized cross section, draw individual dental
arch and reconstruct planes through teeth centers).
Therefore, the proposed pipeline consists of a pre‐
processing module, a tooth instance segmentation mod-
ule and a radial plane reconstruction module corre-
sponding to the aforementioned steps, and expert‐level
annotations were used for model training to gain model
explainability and generalization ability.
A pre‐processing module was designed to reduce the
dimension to emulate the process of optimized cross‐
section selection. In the pre‐processing module, the
Hounsfield Units (HU) value of CBCTs was adjusted as
−1024~3072, followed by the MIP from the sagittal di-
rection to reduce irrelevant information. Harris corner
detection was then employed to identify the upper‐left

and lower‐left corner points of MIP corresponding to the
maxillary and mandibular CEJ levels. Cross‐sectional
slices of five layers above and lower CEJ levels were
collected as proposed sets to resist heterogeneities.
The second module mimicked the expert drawing of
individual dental arch curves by clearly outlining teeth
on cross sections. The cross‐section sets were input to the
tooth instance segmentation module. Three deep learning
models
(Mask
DINO,[26]
Mask2Former,[27]
Mask
RCNN[28]) were trained using tooth annotations labeled
by a senior dentist. Particularly, the Mask RCNN model
first proposed multiple regions of interest (ROIs), then
classified the ROIs into different instances and generated
tooth masks. When the IoU at the same tooth sites be-
tween adjacent cross sections exceeded 0.5, the root
alignment operation aligned masks across all sections to
amend the mis‐classifications. The optimized maxillary
and mandibular cross sections were selected that dis-
played the most classifications and the largest tooth area.
In the last module, which referred to the manual
plane reconstructions along teeth centers, individualized
maxillary and mandibular dental arch curves were
depicted by connecting all teeth geometrical centers.
Based on the normal direction of dental arch curves and
coordinates of teeth centers, serial tooth‐centric radial
planes were resliced using SimpleITK. The resolutions of
the tooth‐centric radial planes are 512  404 and
620  360 pixels on the main and external centers
respectively (Figure 2).
5.3
|
Evaluation of the tooth instance
segmentation
The AI pipeline was trained and validated on the internal
cohort with a data splitting ratio of 4:1, and tested on the
external cohort. Quantitative metrics were evaluated on
cross sections at the CEJ level, including PA, Dice co-
efficients and mIoU. Heatmaps of the quantitative met-
rics were visualized using the pheatmap package in R
(Bell Laboratories, US).
5.4
|
Evaluation of the accuracy in
dental arch curve depiction
Optimized cross sections for dental arch curve depiction
were selected using the segmentation information. Con-
sistency between the manual and AI selected optimized
planes was assessed via Bland‐Altman plots. The point‐
to‐point alignment error of the dental arch curves was
calculated as the mean deviation between the automati-
cally and the manually labeled dental arch curves.[8]
5.5
|
Evaluation of the tooth‐centric
radial planes reconstruction
The localization errors between the AI‐reconstructed and
the GT planes were measured in terms of angular errors
and distance errors. The angular error refers to the angle
between the normal vectors of the two planes, while the
distance error is calculated as the absolute difference in
the minimum distances from the planes to the coordinate
system center. The reconstruction quality was qualita-
tively compared in various tooth sites and oral diseases.
5.6
|
Evaluation of clinical utilities of
the tooth‐centric radial planes
Clinical utility evaluation included the image quality
rating, random and paired confusion experiments and
clinical biometric analysis. The image quality of the AI‐
reconstructed and GT planes was rated by a senior and
junior specialist (>10 and 5–10 years of clinical experi-
ence, respectively) using a five grade scale based on the
clarity of anatomical features (Supporting Information
S1: Table S1). Images rated ≥3 points were considered
clinically qualified, and the qualified rate over total im-
ages was calculated.
In
the
random
confusion
experiments,
20
AI‐
reconstructed and 20 GT planes from different in-
dividuals were randomly presented to junior and senior
specialists for image type identification. In the paired
confusion, 20 pairs of AI‐reconstructed and GT planes with
hidden types were provided for identification. Confusion
matrices of experts' identifications were calculated.
Clinical utility was analyzed by measuring the dental
biometrics in different regions.[7] A total of 11 biometrics
were measured at representative teeth #11 and #21
(anterior maxilla), teeth #16 and #26 (posterior maxilla)
and teeth #36 and #46 (posterior mandible), respectively
(Figure 5d). Measurements on the AI‐reconstructed and
GT planes were compared.
To validate the proposed AI pipeline for fully auto-
matic clinical tasks, a deep learning utility experiment
was conducted. The AI‐reconstructed and GT radial
planes of teeth #11 and #21 were inputted to a previously
developed ResNeXt‐101 algorithm.[29] The ResNeXt‐101
algorithm was trained to be able to automatically
analyze the image features from the sagittal section of
dental CBCT, and predict three tooth‐related biometrics
in an end‐to‐end regression manner, including sagittal
root angle along tooth axis (AngleT), sagittal root angle
along bone axis (AngleB) and their coagulation. The
predictions from the AI‐reconstructed and the GT planes
were compared.

Statistical analyses
Quantitative data were analyzed using SPSS (Version 26,
IBM, US). The paired student's t test was used for
comparing the mean values of the paired samples. The
Wilcoxon signed rank test was used for the ranked data
comparisons. The significance level was set at 0.05 for all
tests.

Abstract: Owing to the tooth‐centered nature of most oral diseases, the tooth‐centric radial plane of cone‐beam computed tomography (CBCT) depicts the anatomical and pathological features along the long axis of the tooth, serving as a crucial imaging modality in the diagnosis, treatment planning, and prognosis of multiple oral diseases. However, reconstructing these standard planes from CBCT is labor‐intensive, time‐consuming, and error‐prone due to anatomical variances and multi‐center discrepancies. This study proposes an expertise‐inspired artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline for the reconstruction of the tooth‐centric radial plane. By emulating expert's workflow, this AI pipeline acquires the optimized maxillary and mandibular cross sections, segments the teeth for dental arch curve depiction, and reconstructs dental arch‐defined tooth‐centric radial planes. A total of 420 CBCT scans from two independent centers, comprising both healthy and diseased subjects, were collected for model development and validation. Teeth on the optimized cross sections were explicitly segmented even in the presence of various complex diseases, resulting in precise dental arch curve depictions.
